DEVELOPMENT OF TOURISM IN ANDAMAN & NICOBAR AND LAKSHADWEEP ISLANDS
 
82.       The emerald islands of Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands are like a glittering jewel and have
 gained popularity as unique tourist destinations and a paradise for naturalists.  The precious heritage of ecology and
 culture of these islands is supported by an extremely fragile ecosystem.  Andaman & Nicobar is a group of 572
 emerald islands, islets and rocks out of which 36 islands are inhabited.  The Andaman’s and Nicobar Islands have
 brilliant tropical flora and are thickly forested with evergreen, deciduous rainforest and tropical trees with mangrove
 swamps at the water edge. The sparkling clear water is excellent for snorkeling with increasing opportunity for
 fabulous Scuba diving for beginner and experienced people. The Islands are also a paradise for bird watchers. The
 coral islands of Lakshadweep consists of 36 islands out of which 10 islands are inhabited. Considering the limited
 infrastructure, the administration of these islands propose to promote low volume high value tourist inflow to these
 islands because of the fragile eco-system of the rain forest and under water corals.
 
83.       The Committee during its study visits to these islands discussed the matter of development of tourism with
 the Administration of Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep Islands, Tour/travel Association and the
 Ministry of Tourism in detail. The following points emerging out of the discussion need urgent attention for
 development of tourism in these islands.
 
84.       The Committee wanted to know about the details of policy for development of tourism in these islands and
 coordination amongst various agencies in the Andaman Nicobar Islands, the Ministry of Tourism submitted that
 promotion of tourism in the Andaman & Nicobar islands is primarily the responsibility of the Andaman & Nicobar
 Administration. There is no specific policy of Ministry of Tourism for development of tourism in the islands. 
 However, Ministry of Tourism has already taken up issues with the concerned Ministries/Departments for the
 overall tourism development in the islands, like relaxation of No Development Zone under CRZ regulation for
 tourism infrastructure, relaxation in Resident Area Permits, Tsunami relief measures, extension of LTC for
 Government servants, etc.
 
85.       During the course of discussions, it was brought to the notice of the Committee that due to poor connectivity,
 tourists have to stay at Port Blair, putting extra pressure on the infrastructure there; whereas the facility created at
 other islands remain unutilized.  The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Tourism about the details of
 connectivity to the other islands within Andaman Nicobar Islands and plans of Ministry of Tourism to improve inter-
island connectivity, the Ministry of Tourism stated that it does not have any scheme for providing internal
 connectivity within the Island.  However, Ministry of Tourism provides central financial assistance on the basis of
 project proposals prioritised in consultation with the UT Administration every year under schemes like, Tourist
 Circuits; Product Infrastructure & Destination Development; and Large Revenue Generating projects.
 
86.       The Committee has been informed that the Ministry of Tourism has launched a scheme of ‘Assistance to
 Large Revenue Generating Projects’ for implementation through Private Public Participation and in partnership with
 other Government/semi-Government agencies. Through this scheme, passenger-shipping services could be
 introduced through private public participation or in partnership with other Government/semi-Government agencies
 to mitigate connectivity problems between different islands. The Planning commission has sanctioned a special grant
 for a number of tourism related projects, one of which relates to improving connectivity among the islands.
 Moreover, no proposal for improving connectivity within the Islands has been received by the Ministry of Tourism
 during 2006-07. No project proposals was either prioritized for the year 2005-06 and 2006-07 nor any project
 proposal, complete in all respect, from the Andaman & Nicobar Island Administration has been received for grant of
 Central Financial Assistance during this period. No officer from the UT Administration attended the Review and
 Prioritization meeting held for the years 2006-07. No project proposal submitted by the Andaman and Nicobar
 Islands Administration during the last one and half year is pending with Ministry of Tourism for grant of Central
 Financial Assistance. However, the Ministry of Tourism has sanctioned HAMFEST – a convention of International

18
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/119threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:24:10]
 Amateur Radio Operators at Port Blair during 2005-06 for Rs.6.25 lakh. A concept Note was sent to the Planning
 Commission recommending Rs.76.50 crore for the revival of Tourism in Andaman & Nicobar Islands on the basis of
 which special outlay has been allocated for Andaman & Nicobar Islands by the Planning Commission.
 
87.       The Committee enquired about the participation of private operators in the development of tourism in
 Andaman Nicobar Islands and the details of the incentives/concessions available to the private operators there.
 The Ministry of Tourism informed that a scheme ‘Assistance to Large Revenue Generating Projects’ for
 implementation through Private Public Participation and in partnership with other Government/semi-Government
 agencies has been launched. Through this scheme, private entrepreneurs can take up revenue generating projects
 in the islands, subject to necessary environment and other clearances. The quantum of subsidy under this scheme
 is with a cap of Rs.50 Cr. subject to a maximum of 25% of total project cost or 50% of equity contribution of the
 private promoter, whichever is lower. Ministry of Tourism encourages growth of budget hotel accommodation
 through a scheme of ‘Incentives to Accommodation Infrastructure’ which can be availed of by private
 entrepreneurs for building accommodation units in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
 
88.       On being asked about reintroduction of the LTC scheme to boost the tourism in the Andaman Nicobar
 Islands, the Ministry of Tourism informed that the LTC packages for visiting Andaman & Nicobar Islands is
 administered by the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pension. In order to revive the domestic tourist
 traffic to the Andaman & Nicobar Islands after the Tsunami tragedy, Secretary, Ministry of Tourism had requested
 the Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pension on 10.11.2005 to extend the special LTC
 facility for Central Government Employees for a further period of two years beyond 24.11.2005.
 
89.       The Committee in its sixtieth report on development of tourism in the country had recommended for
 relaxation of Coastal Regulation Zone act for allowing the development of tourism projects in coastal areas
 especially in A&N and Lakshdweep islands. The Committee desired to know the steps taken by the Ministry for
 relaxation of CRZ regulation in Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep Islands. The Ministry of Tourism
 in its reply informed that world class tourism infrastructure should be developed in the Andaman & Nicobar and
 Lakshadweep islands to attract high value low volume tourist traffic, considering the fragile nature and carrying
 capacity of the islands. Ministry of Tourism has emphasized that stringent CRZ restriction will not help in
 establishing world class tourism infrastructure in these islands. At the instance of the Ministry of Tourism, the
 National Coastal Zone Management Authority has reduced the No Development Zone to 50 mtrs instead of 200
 mtrs for the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. According to Ministry of Environment and Forests, relaxation in the No
 Development Zone for Lakshadweep islands upto 5 mtrs is under finalization in consultation with the Centre for
 Earth Science Studies (CESS), Trivandrum, which had taken up the coastal management study for Lakshadweep
 Islands.
 
90.       The Committee notes that as per its recommendations the Ministry of Environment and Forests has reduced the No
 Development Zone to 50 mtrs. instead of 200 mtrs. in Andaman and Nicobar islands.  The proposals for relaxation in No
 Development Zone for Lakshadweep islands upto 5mtrs. is under finalisation. The Committee feels that this move will
 definitely facilitate the development of world class tourism infrastructure in the islands and coastal areas besides attracting
 high value and low volumes tourists traffic in these islands.
91.       During the course of oral evidence the Secretary (Tourism) apprised the Committee about the Island tourism
 that :
 
“There are two or there important issues involved in promotion of island tourism. The most important thing is
 the Environment and Forests Policy of our country. We need to have a harmonious development of both
 promotion of tourism and protection of our fragile environment. We took up this issue with the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests and, after a lot of debate, they have made some concession in respect of Andaman
 group of islands. They had earlier stipulated that there should be no building or development activity, within

18
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/119threport.htm[22-10-2018 12:24:10]
 200 metres, which was subsequently, increased to 500 metres. Now they have agreed that in the case of
 Anmdamans, they would bring it down to 50 mts. So, this is one concession which we have secured from the
 Ministry of Environment and Forests. Subsequently, we wanted to centrally drive this proposal forward to
 promote tourism as such. They have clearly stated that they would consider proposals on case-to-case basis
 and they would examine each proposal from the environment point of view and then give any clearance.
 Then, we went back to the Administration of the islands and said, “With this concession which has now been
 given, you come up with specific proposals.” But so far, to my knowledge, not a single proposal has really
 been processed. We are pursuing it  with the Andaman Administration. As far as Lakshadweep islands are
 concerned, there again, we have requested for relaxation of the Coastal Zone Regulation. This matter has
 been referred to some Institute, and the Institute is now preparing the Coastal Management Plan. Our
 suggestion is that they should reduce it to 5 mts. and provide for onboard facilities there. The Ministry of
 Environment and Forests is yet to take a view on the subject. This is actually one area where both of us, the
 Environment Ministry and the Tourism Ministry, have to strike a balance. We are trying to promote tourism
 and they are trying to protect environment. Actually, in the Andamans, immediately after the beach waters,
 there is forest. There is absolutely no place for private promoters to develop tourism there.”
 
92.       The Committee notes that the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep islands have the potential of
 growing as unique tourist destinations for Eco-Tourism and Island Tourism but due to variety of limitations particularly
 the inadequate connectivity, the tourism in these islands has not grown as required both in the scale and quality.  At
 Andaman the tourists have to largely depend on the infrastructure at Port Blair whereas the facility created at the other
 islands remains unutilized for want of poor inter-islands connectivity. The Committee is constrained to note that inspite
 of the limited resources, the Administration of these islands have not sent any proposals to the Ministry of Tourism for
 release of the central financial assistance for development of the infrastructure as well the connectivity. It clearly shows
 the lackadaisical attitude of the Administrations of these islands. The Committee, therefore, urges the Administrations of
 these islands to prepare concrete proposals complete in all respect for release of central financial assistance under
 different schemes of the Ministry of Tourism for promotion and development of infrastructure as well as connectivity. In
 this way they could encourage the growth of hotel accommodation and mitigate connectivity problems between different
 islands. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Tourism to take up the matter with Administration of these islands
 for sending the proposals so as to createconducive environment of investment and to seek larger flow of funds from
 private sector participation in developing the necessary infrastructure and accommodation and then privately manage it
 through a transparent process
. 
 
93.       The Committee notes that in order to revive the domestic tourists traffic, the Ministry of Tourism has requested
 the DoPT for extension of LTC facility by air for the central government employees for a furtherperiod of 2 years
 beyond24.11.2005. The Committee recommends the Ministry to pursue the matter for extension of LTC facility in the
 Andaman and Nicobar Islands for the central government employees with the DoPT and Ministry of Tourism should
 introduce attractive LTC packages for these employees visiting Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS – AT A GLANCE
 
REVIEW OF ACTIVITIES OF THE 10th PLAN (2002-2007) AND ANALYSIS OF THE
 ANNUAL PLAN (2007-08)
            The Committee is of the opinion that the plan outlay was not sufficient to exploit the tremendous potential of tourism

 the Ministry has been as high as 92.74%. The budgetary allocation of the Ministry made for the entire 10 th plan was not
 given to the Ministry of Tourism. The Committee strongly feels that any cut in the budgetary allocation will have negative
 impact on growth, strengthening of tourism infrastructure and hospitality related services in the country. The Committee
 expects that the Ministry of Tourism will strongly make demand for more allocation of funds for the 11 th Five Year Plan
 and will get the requisite funds for developing the tourism which is the sunrise industry of the
 day.                                                           (Para 8)

 it is evenly spread throughout the year. The States/UTs may be continuously pursued to (i) send their proposals right at the
 beginning of the financial year, (ii) release funds to their Tourism Ministry or Department and furnish quarterly progress

st March 2004, the unspent balances were Rs.184.37 crore as on 1 st April 2005 and outstanding

th Plan could be fully utilized. The Committee desires the Ministry to inform the

 while finalizing the 11
th Plan document on Tourism a holistic and focused approach should be taken for assessment of all

th Five Year

 Rs.2012.91 crore and an amount of Rs.1558.25 crore was released. Out of the sanctioned projects only 441 projects or
 38.11% works could be completed till date and there still remain a shortfall of 716 projects. The Committee is not satisfied
 with the restricted progress of the Ministry in completion of tourism infrastructure development projects. The Committee
 fails to understand as to how the Ministry would achieve the physical and financial targets in the absence of quantifiable
 goals. The Ministry contended that the development of tourism infrastructure projects generally requires 36 months for

HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
            The Committee notes that the hospitality and service sector has been accorded priority with the growth and
 diversification of tourism activities. The Committee further notes that there are five institutes of repute being run in the
 private sector apart from there are 125 institutes of hotel management in the country offering hospitality programmes in
 private sector.  The Committee observes that as a sizeable number of private IHMs have emerged in the country to offer
 courses in hotel management programme there is a need to provide a institutional and integrated course in development of
 the country’s human resources programme. The Committee is pleased to note that although the guidelines for affiliation of
 these private institutes have been put-in place spelling out the eligibility requirements for affiliation though these institutes
 are lacking in training and other infrastructural facilities. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to grant a
 statutory/deemed university status to NCHMCT for achieving excellence in the tourism sector and to standardized the
 quality of education and training through affiliation and academic supervision through an Act of
 Parliament.                                                                        (Para 44)
            The Committee is constrained to note that there is huge demand-supply mismatch of manpower servicing the tourism
 industry resulting in poor quality of service offered to the tourists. The Committee feels that there is a need to develop the
 required human resources in various segments of the tourism industry consequent upon the rapid growth in the tourism,
 rapidly changing technology and a more demanding competitive market. The Committee recommends the Ministry to
 address the issues related to human resources development in the tourism sector with particular emphasis on qualified
 tourists guides, involving the quality of human resources, their condition of works, training and opportunities, the role of
 private sector for efficient administration and successful operation of the quality of manpower.

 domestic and international tourists. The Committee finds that the creation of tourism infrastructure has multiplier effect in

            The Committee notes that the Ministry of Tourism through its overseas offices, attempts to promote India as a
 preferred tourist destination and to increase the number of foreign tourists arrivals in the country. The Committee observes
 that there is strong competition in the tourist generating markets for attracting foreign tourists to their countries. The
 Committee recommends the Ministry to review the functioning of the overseas marketing offices and, if need be relocate
 some of them in view of the emerging tourism requirements of the prospective tourists besides revamping the India tourism
 website to make it more user friendly. The Committee appreciates the work done by the Ministry in the form of Incredible
 India campaign and recommends the Ministry to reinforce the campaign in the global tourist market with more vigor and
 zeal.  The Committee also recommends that Incredible India campaigning should also be done in various regional languages
 to boost domestic tourism.                                 (Para 57)

 attracting tourists although the  foreign tourists and foreign exchange earnings through tourism (in US Dollars), have

 foreign tourists arrivals in the country are inadequate budgetary support for promotion and marketing, non-availability of
 accommodation at the major ports of entry and other major tourist centres in the country during season, fear about health
 and hygiene conditions, perceptions relating to safety and security and expensive packages as compared to many South East
 Asian countries. The Committee recommends the Ministry to lay emphasis on safety, security and hygiene aspects along

 hotels and VAT on food and beverages and on Airline Turbine Fuel (ATF) and high rate of taxation on tourist transport
 vehicles have deterring impact on the growth of tourism. The Committee notes that the issues related to very high and

 existence as an end to economic growth itself.  Culture and creativity manifest themselves in almost all economic, social

 Elements of culture encompass media, films, music, handicrafts, visual arts, performing arts, literature, heritage
 management, cultural and creative industries etc. The Cultural development inter-alia includes areas of culture both in
 tangible and intangible fields.  The functional spectrum of the Ministry of Culture as the nodal executive agency is rather
 wide, ranging from generating cultural awareness at the grassroots level to promoting cultural exchanges at an international
 level. 
 
2.         The Ministry of Culture has six Subordinate Offices, two attached Offices and thirty three Autonomous Bodies and
 two Missions under its purview.  The major areas of activities of the Ministry are Archaeology, Museums, Anthropology
 and Ethnology, Libraries, Archives and Archival Libraries, Dissemination of Art and Culture, Memorials, Centenaries and
 Anniversaries, Buddhist and Tibetan Institutions and International Cultural Relation. The programmes undertaken by the
 Ministry can broadly be classified as, activities of North East Region, Archaeology, Museums, Anthropology and
 Ethnology, Archives and Archival Libraries, Tibetan/Buddhist Studies, Libraries, Akademies and National School of
 Drama, Promotion and Dissemination of Culture, Memorials, Centenaries and Anniversaries, Cultural Relations and
 Festival of India, IGNCA and Secretariat.

3.         Demand No.19 containing the details of budget allocation of the Ministry of Culture for the financial year 2007-08
 was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its
 meeting held on the 5
th April 2007.  During the year 2007-08, the Ministry of Culture has received Plan funds to the tune of
 Rs. 557.00 crore which includes a sum of Rs.50.00 crore as capital outlay.  As regards Non-Plan provision, an attempt has

 recorded continuously as these parameters have a bearing on the behaviour and distribution of pollutants in the

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
Comparison of the 10th and 11th Five Year Plans and overall assessment of financial performance for the years 2006-
07 and 2007-08:
 
The Committee notes that while comparing B.E. 2006-07 and B.E. 2007-08, it is observed that most of the major
 schemes under the Ministry of Culture have got  increased allocations.  The Committee feels that preservation and
 protection of vast cultural resources of the country is a task gigantic in nature and requires huge investments.  But, the
 Committee is at dismay that the Government has always treated it as non productive sector thereby inviting apathy of the
 Finance Ministry which is always reducing the allocations made for the Ministry of Culture at Revised Estimates stage.  
 The Committee strongly feels that this sector is catalytic for economic growth and not only that but also preservation of our
 culture means preserving our national identity which should not be compromised at any cost.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the allocations made for the year 2007-08 should not be reduced at RE stage by the Finance Ministry and
 the Ministry of Culture should try to spend the allocations to the fullest extent. 
 
            Our culture is the most vibrant and rich culture in the world.  The Committee feels that culture has to be harnessed
 together with tourism and showcased to the world.  The right modal mix between culture and tourism would yield valuable
 foreign exchange by inviting more and more tourists; promote our artists and artisans many of whom are at the verge of
 starvation; preserve our local/ regional culture, art and craft ; last but not the least, it will also enthuse private sector to
 invest more and more in these activities.  The Committee strongly recommends that the approach of the Ministry of Culture,
 Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission should change during the 11
th Five Year Plan and all of them should
 together take adequate care and ensure that none of the Plan activities in respect of Ministry of Culture and its organizations
 is deferred due to reduction in Annual Plan outlay at the stage of Revised Estimates. 
 
            The Committee strongly recommends its earlier observations with regard to budgeting pattern of the Ministry of
 Culture and reiterates its recommendations made at para 11 of the 103
rd Report on the Demands for Grants for the year
 2006-07 wherein it was stated that :-
 
"The Committee is of the view that fixing of the Revised Estimates ceiling by the Ministry of Finance on the basis of
 the level of expenditure attained upto the month of September/October creates problem for the Department of
 Culture.   The Committee observes that most of the cultural functions and festivals take place in the month of
 October and November, after the monsoon.  The Archaeological Survey of India also incurs major expenditure after
 the monsoon.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government must review the budgeting procedure and
 evolve some mechanism to ensure that the Plan allocation for the Department of Culture is not reduced.  The

General of ASI which is resulting in the neglect of this premier institution. The Committee reiterates its earlier

Archaeological Survey of India (ASI)
 
(a)   Conservation and Preservation of Monuments:
(b)   Excavations & Explorations
 
            The Committee recommends that conservation preservation work undertaken by ASI including phase II of Ajanta
 Ellora project should be completed within a definite time frame and in a targeted manner.  The details and outcome of these
 may be provided to the Committee separately. As regards exploration and excavations, the Committee feels that selection of
 new sites is a welcome step but this should also be done in a systematic and time bound manner.  Moreover, findings of
 excavations should also be recorded simultaneously so that the report is finalized by the end of the excavation work itself. 
 The Committee strongly recommends that the pending reports on excavations undertaken by ASI should be finalized and
 published without any loss of time.
            The Committee notes that conservation of our heritage is important, both for encouraging tourism as well as for
 attracting visitors from overseas.  The importance of cultural tourism in the context of development of both culture and
 tourism cannot be overemphasized.  Archaeological Survey of India, which is a flagship organization of the Ministry of
 Culture is engaged in conservation, preservation and maintenance of monuments.  Unless and until substantive allocation of
 funds is made to ASI towards undertaking the massive task of maintenance and conservation of heritage, ancient
 monuments and historical sites, the heritage preservation in a sustained manner and promotion of ancient cultural heritage
 could not be achieved.  Unfortunately, this aspect of heritage preservation/promotion has received very little attention it
 deserves.  This is due to meagre Plan budget of the Ministry which acts as a constraint to step up its activities.  Therefore,
 the Committee recommends that more funds allocation should be made to ASI and number of monuments under its
 protection should also be increased taking into account the total number of unprotected monuments in the country which are
 languishing and dithering due to neglect.
(Paras 22 & 23)

 fixed for achieving the stated objective so that the allocation made for this purpose is not wasted.    The Committee also
 recommends that in addition to the four States chosen initially for the purpose activities of the Mission should also be
 extended to other States which are economically backward but culturally very rich.

 REPORT
 
            The National Waterway (Talcher-Dhamra Stretch of Rivers Geonkhali-Charbatia Stretch of East Coast Canal,
 Charbatia-Dhamra Stretch of Matai River and Mahanadi Delta Rivers) Bill, 2006 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on
 8th December, 2006. On 13 th December, 2006, the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Hon'ble
 Speaker, Lok Sabha referred the Bill to this Committee for examination  and Report.  Under the mandate, the
 Committee has examined the Bill and finalised the Report.  The Bill seeks to provide for the declaration of the  Talcher-
Dhamra stretch of Brahmani-Kharsua-Dhamra rivers, Geonkhali-Charbatia stretch of East Coast Canal, Charbatia-
Dhamra stretch of Matai river and Mahanadi delta rivers between Mangalgadi and Paradip in the States of West Bengal
 and Orissa to be a national waterway and also to provide for the regulation and development of the said stretch of the
 rivers and the canals for purpose of shipping and navigation on the said waterway and for matters connected therewith
 or incidental thereto.
2.       In Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the Government have enumerated the objects to be achieved by
 this legislation.
2.1       In the absence of suitable organization and paucity of resources with the State Governments, the development of
 Inland Water Transport (IWT) has not made much headway. There are certain advantages in this mode of transport,
 such as low cost transport, energy efficiency, generation of employment among weaker sections of the community and
 its eco-friendly nature. Various committees set up by the Government for the purpose of looking into this matter had in
 the past recommended that the Central Government should declare certain waterways as national waterways and

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/121streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:26:12]
 assume responsibility for their development. The Central Government have accordingly constituted the Inland
 Waterways Authority of India under the Inland Waterways Authority of India Act, 1985 for the regulation and
 development of inland waterways for purposes of shipping and navigation. Allahabad-Haldia stretch of the Ganga-
Bhagirathi-Hooghly River, Sadiya-Dhubri stretch of the Brahmaputra river and Kollam-Kottappuram stretch of West
 Coast Canal along with Champakkara and Udyogamandal Canals have already been declared as national waterways.
 Consequently, Inland Waterways Authority of India has taken up the development, maintenance and management of
 these waterways.
2.2       The Department of Shipping proposes to declare Talcher-Dhamra stretch of the Brahmani-Kharsua-Dhamra
 rivers, Goenkhali-Charbatia stretch of the East Coast Canal, Charbatia-Dhamra stretch of the Matai river and Mahanadi
 delta rivers between Mangalgadi and Paradip as a National Waterway. Infrastructural facilities currently available on
 this waterway are not adequate for safe, convenient and sustained shipping and navigation by large mechanized crafts.
 Therefore, the waterway is required to be suitably developed by providing adequate infrastructure for safe, convenient
 and sustained shipping operations. The regulation and development of the proposed national waterway under the
 control of the Union for the purposes of shipping and navigation is in the public interest and declaration to that effect
 has also been made in this Bill.
 
3.          The Department of Shipping in their background note furnished to the Committee informed that Inland Water
 Transport is an economic, fuel efficient, environment friendly and employment oriented mode of transport. The role of
 the Union Government is to regulate shipping and navigation on Inland Waterways declared by Parliament by Law to
 be national waterways. The responsibility and executive authority for development and maintenance of all waterways
 other than those declared as National Waterways rests with the State Governments. The following inland waterways
 have so far been declared as National Waterways through Acts of Parliament:
 
(i)
                  Allahabad-Haldia stretch (1620 kms.) of the Ganga-Bhagirathi Hooghly river system by the National
 Waterways (Allahabad-Haldia stretch of Ganga-Hooghly river) Act, 1982;
(ii)                Sadiya-Dhubri stretch (891 kms.) of Brahmputra river by the National Waterway (Sadiya-Dhubri stretch of
 the Brahmputra river) Act, 1988; and
(iii)               Kottapuram-Kollam stretch of the West Coast canal alogwith Champkara canal and Udyogmandal canal
 (205 kms.) by the National Waterway (Kollam-Kottapuram stretch of West Cost Canal and Champakara and
 Udyogmandal canal) Act, 1992.
 
3.1       The Central Government has constituted Inland Waterways Authority of India for development, maintenance
 and regulation of National Waterways for shipping and navigation. The infrastructure facilities on the existing three
 National Waterways are being created by it. It is aimed to make these three National Waterways fully functional by
 2007-08.
3.2       It is now proposed to declare Talcher-Dhamra stretch of the Brahmani-Kharsua-Dhamra river system,
 Geonkhali-Charbatia stretch of the East Coast Canal, Charbatia-Dhamra stretch of the Matai River and Mangalgadi-
Paradip stretch of the Mahanadi delta rivers as National Waterway. (Annexure – I) The waterway under consideration
 comprises river and canal sections having a total length of 623 km falling in the States of West Bengal (91 km) and
 Orissa (532 km) with following break-up:-
Name of River/Canal Length in km
East Coast Canal (Geonkhali-Charbatia)                                  217
Matai River (Charbatia-Dhamra)                                               40
River Brahmani (Talcher-Dhamra)                                            265
Mahanadi Delta Rivers (Mangalgadi-Paradip)              101
                   Total                   623
 

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/121streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:26:12]
3.3       The Department of Shipping informed that the infrastructure currently available on this waterway is not adequate
 for safe, convenient and sustained shipping and navigation by large mechanized crafts. Therefore, the waterway is
 required to be developed by providing adequate infrastructure for safe, convenient and sustained shipping operations. It
 has been visualized that substantial quantum of inland water transport traffic to the tune of 18.07 million tones is likely
 to be carried on the proposed national waterway after its full development in a span of 8 years. This traffic is expected
 to be handled at 4 terminals namely Talcher, Nasirabad, Balasore and Rajnagar. The major identified cargo is coal,
 fertilizer, cement, iron ore, agricultural products, industrial products etc. The proposed dimension of the waterway is:-
For River and Delta portions
                        Bed width                     -                       45 m
                        Depth                           -                       2 m
                        Side slope                    -                       1:5
 
For Canal portion
                        Bed width                     -                       32m
                        Depth                           -                       1.5 m
                        Side slope                    -                       1:2.5
3.4       The canal portion is also propose to be developed to 45 m width during Phase-II, at a later stage. The
 development of the rivers and canals along with provision of infrastructure facilities for purposes of shipping and
 navigation, channel marking, construction of terminals transit sheds, installation of handling equipment, etc. it was
 estimated by the Consultant M/s WAPCOS in the year 2002 that the expenditure with respect to the said development
 will be of the order of Rs.1526 crore (Rs.1282 crore for fairway development + Rs.242 crore for terminals + Rs.2 crore
 for setting up of offices). The expected period of implementation of the project is 8 years. Besides, annual maintenance
 cost of Rs.59 crore was also estimated by the Consultant for operation of the waterway and terminals. The waterway
 will facilitate movement of 200 tonnes vessel (30 m X 605 m X 1.25 m) for canal portion and 500 tonnes vessel (58 m
 X 9 m X 1.5 m) for river section. It will provide an alternative mode of transportation for movement of commodities
 between ports of Paradip, Dhamra and Haldia/ Kolkata and various hinterland cities namely Talcher, Jenapur, Balasore,
 Charbatia and Mangalgadi. It will also facilitate decongestion of roads & fuel savings, provide better environment
 corridor, ensure better port-hinterland connectivity, generate employment among weaker sections of the society and
 increase tourism activities in the region.
 
4.         In order to have wider consultations, the views of individuals, organizations and institutions on the subject
 matter of the Bill were invited through advertisement in all major dailies and vernacular newspapers in the country. The
 Chief Secretary, Government of West Bengal while furnishing the comments of the State Government of West Bengal
 on the proposed new waterway NW-5 has stated as under:-
           
(i)
                  In order to ensure smooth movement of standard barges having capacity of 1000 to 1500 tonnes, the bed
 width of the canal system in West Bengal portion should be increased from 32 to 45 metres and the depth of
 the canal be also increased from 1.5 to 2 metres.
 
(ii)
                A terminal location is required in the State of West Bengal with adequate development of loading and
 unloading facilities etc. Geonkhali in Purba Medinipur district may be considered as the location for the
 terminal in this State.
 
(iii)
               It will be also be absolutely essential to ensure proper dredging of Rupnarayan River from Geonkhali point
 to Kolagaht point. The total distance from Geonkhali to Kolaghat is 18.5 nautical miles. Regarding the
 approximate volume to be dredged to ensure navigation of barges with depth of 2 metres, BCD is around 3
 million cubic metres in at least 14 locations. Kolkata Port Trust has informed that such dredging will have to
 be executed through Low Drafted Cutter-Suction-Dredger and such equipment are owned by IWAI only and

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/121streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:26:12]
 the dredging work will have to be done by IWAI only.
 
4.1       Similarly, the Government of Orissa, Commerce and Transport Department has informed the Committee that the
 Government of Orissa agrees to opening of proposed National Waterway and fully supports the Bill.
 
5.         The Committee pointed out that the existing National Waterways in the country are under utilized and desired to
 know the reasons for declaration of the new waterways and the strategy conceived to popularize the IWT mode in the
 country, the Department of Shipping in their reply informed the Committee that like any other transport sector, inland
 waterways also require basic infrastructure facilities namely assured navigation channel with adequate depth and width,
 terminals for berthing of vessels and loading and unloading of cargo and navigational aids for round the clock operation
 of inland vessels. Though some infrastructure has been provided on the three National Waterways, it has not reached a
 threshold level to become commercially viable. Due to this, the waterways are not being utilized to their potential.
 However, cargo is being transported on the three national waterways and an increasing trend is also visible as given
 below:
             
                                                              (in billion tonne km)
Cargo Transportation 2003-04 2004-05 2005-06
NW-1 0.160 0.312 0.411
NW-2 0.029 0.025 0.032
NW-3 0.022 0.015 0.017
Total 0.211 0.352 0.460
 
6.         IWAI has now made an Action Plan to make these National Waterways fully functional subject to availability of
 funds. Utilization of the National Waterways thereafter is expected to increase substantially, as also operations on these
 waterways will become commercially viable. For demonstrating the functionality of the three NWs and increasing the
 confidence level of IWT operators, IWAI has also planned fixed Schedule Service (FSS) for demonstrative purpose on
 the three NWs, which will be operated by cargo vessels acquired by IWAI. This level of development of the existing
 National Waterways will be the ‘Stage-1’ of the development where basic infrastructure will be put in place through
 pubic investment, and private investment will be mainly for operation of IWT vessels. Thereafter, further upgradation
 of infrastructure e.g. developing higher LAD, specialized terminals could take place through private investment. This
 upgradation can be termed as ‘Stage-2’ development. The ‘Stage-1’ development will require 2 to 3 years for putting
 up infrastructure and further 3-4 years for demonstration of functionality after which the ‘Stage-2’ development will be
 mainly through private investment and role of IWAI/Government will be that of facilitator and regulator only.
 
7.         IWT is a fuel efficient, cost effective and environment friendly mode of transport. With adequate investment and
 focus it can be developed into a viable and visible mode complementary to the rail and road modes. Due attention has
 not been paid in the past to the IWT mode, but now the Union Government intends to develop it fast and as a part of
 this effort two new waterways have been identified for declaration as new National Waterways. It is planned that while
 existing National Waterways are being made fully functional under Stage-1 development, the procedural formalities
 would be gone through and Parliamentary approval would be obtained for declaration of new National Waterways, so
 that projects on these are approved and they become ready for Stage-1 development, thereby maintaining a continuity
 in IWT development in the country. In other words, when the existing three National Waterways would be in Stage-2
 development mode, the proposed new National Waterways will be developed under Stage-1 and after their Stage-1
 development, they also will be ready for Stage-2 development.
 
8.         The waterways other than National Waterways will also be developed through the respective State Governments
 for which liberal funding is available under Centrally Sponsored Scheme as of now. This approach will lead to overall
 development of IWT sector in the country. As far as enhancing utilization of existing and proposed National Waterway
 is concerned, apart from demonstrative cargo operation for ascertaining functional characteristics of the waterways and
 increasing the level of confidence of users, other promotional measures such as inland vessel building subsidy, viability
 gap funding for profitable operators, setting-up of vessel leasing company and other incentives for increased use of the
 waterways would be provided in a phased manner depending upon the requirement from time to time.
 
9.         The Committee wanted to know whether the proposed National Waterway will have any impact on irrigation

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/121streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:26:12]
 interest of the region, in reply, the Department of Shipping informed that the East Cost Canal (which is a part of
 proposed National Waterway-5) was already designed as irrigation cum navigation canal and under the existing
 proposal also, no development is proposed which will adversely affect irrigation interests of the region. Further, IWAI
 had been in continuous touch with all the concerned State Governments of the proposed National Waterway at various
 stages and their views have been considered while planning development works. Therefore, it is confirmed that
 irrigation interests of the concerned States will not be compromised due to development of proposed National
 Waterway.
 
10.       The Committee wanted to know as to how the IWT vessels would be serviced and repaired when large number
 of vessels starts plying on existing three National Waterways and proposed two National Waterways. The Department
 of Shipping submitted that the Coastal areas of the existing and proposed National Waterways namely Kolkata in case
 of NW-1, Kochi in case of NW-3 and Kakinada, Chennai, Visakhapatnam and Paradip etc. in case of NW-4 and 5
 already have repair facilities which can cater to the repair needs of inland vessels. On NationalWaterway No. 1 and 2
 however, adequate repair facilities do not exist on inland stations like Patna, Varanasi, Allahabad (NW-1) and
 Guwahati (NW-2). Therefore, under the Action Plan of IWAI for making three National Waterways fully functional,
 projects for construction of repair facilities at Patna and Guwahati are also being prepared.  When the IWT vessels start
 plying in large numbers on these waterways it is expected that repair facilities will also grow based on the demand,
 propelled by market forces.
 
11.       The Committee wanted to know as to how this particular waterway will benefit the people of West Bengal and
 Orissa. The Department of Shipping informed that potential of inland water transport (IWT) corridors if developed with
 required IWT infrastructure namely fairway, navigational aids and terminals, can offer alternative/supplementary mode
 of transport vis-à-vis rail and road modes. Since waterways generally do not provide door-to-door service
 independently, it is necessary that these are connected with rail and/or road mode for total transport linkages to the user.
 
12.       The Committee was further informed that each IWT corridor (waterways) has specific characteristics and
 developmental needs, to become viable mode of transport. Several Committees (viz. Gokhale Committee, Bhagavati
 Committee and National Transport Policy Committee) have studied IWT system of the country since independence
 from time to time and have advocated systematic development of the IWT mode. National Transport Policy Committee
 in its report (1980) accordingly recommended for setting up of an authority for development and regulation of inland
 waterways. Accordingly, Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) was constituted in October, 1986. Techno-
economic feasibility studies have been made for different waterways from time to time, which establish viability of this
 mode by developing a particular waterway with above stated IWT infrastructure to act as supplementary/alternative
 mode.  Further, the proposed National Waterway-5 will impact positively the rural economy and provide IWT
 connectivity to the existing National Waterway-1 (the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly system) and the Indo-
BangladeshProtocol route through Sunderbans. It will also provide for an alternative mode of transport for movement of
 commodities between ports of Paradip, Dhamra and Haldia/Kolkata and various hinterland towns namely Talcher,
 Jenapur, Balasore, Charbatia and Mangalgadi. It will also help in decongestion of roads, provide port-hinterland
 connectivity, generate employment and increase tourism activities in the region.
 
13.       The Department of Shipping further submitted that the fundamental requirement for growth of IWT sector is
 development of waterways with basic IWT infrastructure namely fairway with adequate depth, navigational aids for
 day and night navigation and terminals with mechanical handling facilities and connectivity with rail and road to enable
 the waterways to provide a cost effective mode of transport. However, ownership and operation of cargo and passenger
 vessels should be in private hands. Therefore, in addition to putting up infrastructure, it is also required to provide
 necessary conditions conducive to private sector participation in IWT operations. IWAI is concentrating on providing
 full infrastructure in the existing National Waterways in order to make them fully functional. The following
 steps/measures are also being taken up for giving boost to Inland Water Transport Sector:
 
·
        Encouraging private sector in development, operation and management of IWT infrastructures.
 
·        Providing facilitative framework for increasing IWT fleet under private ownership by way of providing
 Inland Vessel Building Subsidy and forming Inland Vessel Leasing Company with the support of financial

REPORT
file:///D/responive/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/121streport.htm[22-10-2018 12:26:12]
 institutions and private sector.
 
·        Attracting/promoting cargo transportation by IWT mode by way of demonstrative voyages/fixed schedule
 sailings by IWAI, attracting multi-modal operators to IWT and providing funding for operating IWT
 vessels.
 
·        Encouraging States to develop their potential waterways through liberal assistance under Centrally
 Sponsored Scheme.
 
 
14.       The Department of Shipping informed that no freight subsidy is being provided to IWT sector as of now.
 However, it would be desirable to provide a reasonable freight subsidy in the initial stages of IWT development to
 attract private sector in ownership and operation of IWT vessel for cargo. Accordingly, a package of incentives
 (including subsidy for operation) to be extended to IWT sector is under consideration with the Government. The
 Committee has also been informed that for encouraging private investment in IWT sector, several fiscal incentives have
 been approved in the IWT Policy, 2001. These include (i) Joint Venture by IWAI (ii) Equity participation by
 Government in BOT project (iii) Tax exemption similar to National Highways (iv) Enhancement in depreciation rates
 for inland vessels (v) Vessel building subsidy of 30% and (vi) Custom duty concession.  For attracting private
 investment in IWT sector through JVs with IWAI, IWAI Act was also amended. Thereafter, M/s IFCI Ltd. was
 appointed by IWAI as Consultant to assist IWAI. M/s IFCI Ltd. identified some priority projects and prepared bid
 documents thereto. Some of these projects were thereafter advertised and these have resulted in positive response.
 IWAI has recently signed MoUs for setting up of three jetties at Bandel, Kolaghat and Budge-Budge in West Bengal
 for fly ash handling (estimated cost of these three jetties is Rs.2.70 crore) and also three major projects for ownership,
 operation and management of barges on identified O-D routes namely; Kolkata-Mongla (8 barges of 2000 DWT each
 for transportation of 1,45,000 tonne of fly ash, jute, foodgrains etc. annually total estimated investment Rs.44 crore),
 Pandu-Kolkata (6 barges of 2000 DWT each for transportation of 65,000 tonne of tea, jute, cement and bitumen
 annually total estimated investment Rs.33 crore) and Dhubri-Kolkata (2 barges of 1500 DWT each for transportation of
 22,000 tonne of jute, cement and salt annually total estimated investment Rs.10 crore). The requisite infrastructure on
 this waterway (East Coast Canal from Talcher-Dhamra stretch of rivers, Geonkhali-Dhamra stretch of Matai river and
 Mahanadi delta rivers) are proposed to be provided by the Central Govt. However, the vessels are expected to be
 procured and operated by private entrepreneurs by availing the inland vessel building subsidy scheme and other
 incentives provided/ to be provided Private investment is unlikely if the basic minimum infrastructure is not in position.
 Hence, private investment is not expected on this waterway till requisite infrastructure is developed through public
 funding.
 
15.       As regards overall region-wise plan for development of these waterways, the Department of Shipping intimated
 that out of the total length of 623 km of the proposed waterway, 91 km falls in West Bengal and the balance portion of
 532 km in Orissa. The river portion of the waterway (i.e. Brahmani river, Matai river and Mahanadi delta river) is
 proposed to be developed for a fairway of 45 m bottom width and 2 m depth and the East Coast Canal portion with 32
 m bottom width and depth of 1.5 m. Terminals are proposed to the set up at Talcher in river Brahmani, Nasirabad and
 at Balasore in the East Coast Canal and at Rajnagar in Mahanadi delta portion. Once fully developed, the waterway
 would be operational for 24 hrs navigation. The techno-economic feasibility (TEF) study for the project has been
 carried out through the Consultant M/s WAPCOS, New Delhi during 1998. The feasibility study had made a projected
 cargo to the tune of 11.07 million ton, 13.75 million tons and 18.07 million tons for the 1
st year, 5th year and 10th year
 after fully developing the waterway. In order to get the present status a study for preparation of DPR is underway
 through the Consultant, M/s WAPCOS. The planning and implementation of the project would be made based on the
 project components identified as per the DPR study. Requisite monitoring system will be worked out after declaration
 of the waterway as a National Waterway.
 
16.       On a query regarding the estimated cost for development of these waterways, the Department of Shipping
 intimated that the project cost is estimated at Rs.1526 crore (2002 rate). Besides, recurring cost to the tune of Rs.59
 crore is also estimated to carry out annual maintenance of fairway, barrages and terminals. The Consultant has
 estimated that Rs.293 crore annual earnings will be generated in the initial years (after full development of the

 berthing charges, mooring charges, storage/warehousing charges, lock charges etc. It is estimated that waterway will be
 made fully functional within a period of 9 years after its declaration.
 
17.       The Committee wanted to know whether the Department of Shipping has consulted the Governments of West
 Bengal and Orissa before introduction of Bills. In their reply, the Department of Shipping informed that the issue of
 declaration of proposed waterway as National Waterway was discussed in the Maritime State Development Council

 with copies of Detailed Project Report of the Project for preparing an action plan for cargo generation in the proposed
 National Waterway. Copies of the Detailed Project Report (Draft Final Report) were provided to both the State
 Governments by the IWAI on 17.1.2006. Besides, before introducing the Bill in the Parliament, the Minister of
 Shipping, Road Transport and Highways has written a letter dated 25.8.2006 to the Chief Minister of West Bengal and
 the Chief Minister of Orissa about intention of the Government to declare the proposed waterway as a National

18.       As regards the riparian dispute, the Department of Shipping submitted that the Department is not aware of any
 riparian dispute between the State Governments in the region. The fairway development (for navigation) will be done
 without hampering the existing water usages including irrigation interest of both the States.
 
19.       On a specific query as to why State Governments are not taking interest in the development and maintenance of
 IWT sector, the Department of Shipping intimated that IWT sector remained neglected in the entire country for a very
 long time due to which Central Government as well as State Governments did not give priority for its development.
 After formation of IWAI in October, 1986 attention was given for development of National Waterways by the Central
 Government State Governments however, continued to neglect development of waterways (other than National
 Waterways) probably due to fund constraints. After revision of assistance pattern under Central Sponsored Scheme for
 IWT development in October, 2002 where 100% grant to NE States and 90% grant to other States was made applicable,
 many States have already shown great interest in development of IWT mode. From 2003-04 onwards, 33 projects of 14
 States have been sanctioned by the Central Government and Rs.48 crore have also been released to these States for
 execution of sanctioned projects.
 
20.       The Committee has been informed that considering the interests shown by the States in developing IWT sector
 through revised Central Sponsored Scheme, it is necessary that this scheme is continued on a long term basis to
 generate further confidence among the States. It is also necessary that IWT organization in all the Riverine and Coastal
 States through fora such as Maritime States Development Council (MSDC), IWT Development Council and interaction
 done by IWAI with these States. In addition, concerned States are continuously consulted/ involved in development of
 existing National Waterways as well as in the preparation of development plans for other waterways.
 
21.       The Committee has consistently expressed its concern over the slow pace of development of IWT sector in the
 country. The Committee once again notes that IWT is one of the oldest, fuel efficient, cost-effective and environment
 friendly mode of transport but unfortunately the potential of IWT remains largely unexplored due to the indifferent
 attitude of the Central and State Governments. The Committee observes that although the Department of Shipping is
 committed to increase the share of IWT in the country’s total EXIM trade, still the waterways are not being utilized to
 their potential and remain largely neglected and underdeveloped for want of required infrastructure namely fairways,
 terminals and navigable aids, as a result, it has not reached at a threshold level to become commercially viable. The
 committee is of the firm view that with adequate investments, policy framework and focused approach, the IWT in the
 country can be developed into a viable mode complementary to the rail and road modes. The Committee is of the
 opinion that if the Government really intends to develop the IWT sector with fast pace to its full potential in the country
 then it should sincerely endeavour to provide institutional framework and minimize the procedural bottlenecks besides
 providing adequate investments both from public and private partnership and to develop it to a level where private
 sector feels confident to invest in this sector particularly in ownership and operation of cargo and passenger vessels to
 IWT mode. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to provide institutional framework for
 development of IWT sector in the country so as to increase the capacity of IWT agencies, commercialization of IWT
 industries, increased cost recovery through user charges and creation of a vibrant IWT sector in the country.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
            In the absence of suitable organization and paucity of resources with the State Governments, the
 development of Inland Water Transport has not made much headway. There are certain advantages in this mode
 of transport, such as, low cost transport, energy efficiency, generation of employment among weaker sections of
 the community and its eco-friendly nature. Various committees set up by the Government for the purpose of
 looking into this matter recommended that the Central Government should declare certain waterways as national
 waterway sand assume responsible for their development.
            2.  The Central Government have accordingly constituted the Inland Waterways Authority of India under
 the Inland Waterways Authority of India Act, 1985 (82 of 1985), for the regulation and development of inland
 waterways for purposes of shipping and navigation. Allahabad-Haldia stretch of the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly
 River, Sadiya-Dhubri stretch of the Brahmaputra river and Kollam-Kottappuram stretch of West Coast Canal
 along with Champakkara and Udyogamandal Canals have already been declared as national waterways by the
 National Waterway (Allahabad-Haldia Stretch of the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly River) Act, 1982 (49 of 1982),
 the National Waterway (Sadiya-Dhubri Stretch of the Brahmaputra River) Act, 1988 and the National
 Waterway (Kollam-Kottappuram Stretch of West Coast Canal and Champakkara and Udyogamandal Canals)
 Act, 1992 (25 of 1992), respectively. Consequently, Inland Waterways Authority of India has taken up the
 development, maintenance and management of these waterways.
            3.  It is now proposed to declare Talcher-Dhamra stretch of the Brahmani-Kharsua-Dhamra rivers,
 Goenkhali-Charbatia stretch of the East Coast Canal, Charbatia-Dhamra stretch of the Matai river and Mahanadi
 delta rivers between Mangalgadi and Paradip as a National Waterway. Infrastructural facilities currently
 available on this waterway are not adequate for safe, convenient and sustained shipping and navigation by large
 mechanized crafts. Therefore, the waterway is required to be developed by providing adequate infrastructure for
 safe, convenient and sustained shipping operations. The regulation and development of the proposed national
 waterway under the control of the Union for the purposes of shipping and navigation is in the public interest and
 declaration to that effect has also been made in this Bill.
            4.  The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

 Waterways Authority of India constituted under the Inland Waterways Authority of India Act, 1985 (82 of
 1985). Consequently, three distinct functions namely, development, maintenance and management of the
 proposed waterway will devolve on the Inland Waterways Authority of India. It has been visualized that inland
 water transport traffic to the tune of 18.07 million tones is likely to be carried on the proposed national
 waterway after its full development by the year 2016-17. This traffic is expected to be handled at 4 terminals
 namely, Talcher, Nasirbad, Balasore and Rajnagar. The development of the rivers and canals along with
 provision of infrastructural facilities for purposes of shipping and navigation to handle the above mentioned

 development will be of the order of Rs.1526.00 crores which will be of a non-recurring nature.

REPORT
            The National Waterway (Kakinada-Pondicherry Stretch of Canals and the Kaluvelly Tank, Bhadrachalam-
Rajahmundry Stretch of River Godavari and Wazirabad-Vijayawada Stretch of River Krishna) Bill, 2006 was
 introduced in the Lok Sabha on 8
th December, 2006. On 13 th December, 2006 Hon'ble Chairman Rajya Sabha, in
 consultation with the Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha referred the Bill to this Committee for examination and Report. 
 Under the mandate, the Committee has examined the Bill and finalised the Report. The Bill seeks to provide for the
 declaration of the Kakinada-Pondicherry stretch of canals comprising of Kakinada  canal, Eluru canal, Commamur 
 canal, Buckingham canal and the Kaluvelly tank, Bhadrachalam-Rajahmundry stretch of river Godavari and
 Wazirabad-Vijayawada stretch of river Krishna in the States of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu and the Union
 Territory of Puducherry to be a national waterway and also to provide for the regulation and development of the said
 stretch of the rivers and the canals for purpose of shipping and navigation on the said waterway and for matters
 connected therewith or incidental thereto.
2.       In the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the Government have enumerated the objects to be achieved
 by this legislation. 
 
2.1       In the absence of suitable organisation and paucity of resources with the State Governments, the development of
 Inland Water Transport (IWT) has not made much headway in those parts of the country where it has vast potentials. 
 There are certain advantages in this mode of transport, such as low cost transport, energy efficiency, generation of
 employment among weaker sections of the society and its eco-friendly nature.  Various committees set up by the
 Government for the purpose of looking into this matter had in the past recommended that the Central Government
 should declare certain waterways as national waterways and assume responsibility for their overall development. The
 Central Government has accordingly constituted the Inland Waterways Authority of India under the Inland Waterways
 Authority of India Act, 1985, for the regulation and development of inland waterways for purposes of shipping and
 navigation.  Allahabad-Haldia stretch of the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly River, Sadiya-Dhubri stretch of the
 Brahmaputra river and Kollam-Kottappuram stretch of West Coast Canal along with Champakkara and Udyogamandal
 Canals have already been declared as national waterways. Consequently, Inland Waterways Authority of India has
 taken up the development, maintenance and management of these waterways.
 
2.2       The Department of Shipping proposes to declare Kakinda-Puducherry stretch of canals comprising of Kakinada
 Canal, Eluru Canal, Commamur Canal, Buckingham Canal and Kaluvelly Tank along with Bhadrachalam-
Rajahmundry stretch of Godavari river and Wazirabad-Vijayawada stretch of the Krishna river as a National Waterway,
 Infrastructure facilities currently available on this waterway are not adequate for safe, convenient and sustained
 shipping and navigation by large mechanized crafts.  Therefore, the waterway is required to be suitably developed by
 providing adequate infrastructure for safe, convenient and sustained shipping operations.  The regulation and
 development of the proposed national waterway under the control of the Union for the purposes of shipping and
 navigation is in the public interest and declaration to that effect has also been made in this Bill.
3.         The Department of Shipping in their background note furnished to the Committee informed that Inland Water
 Transport is an economic, fuel efficient, environment friendly and employment oriented mode of transport. The role of
 the Union Government is to regulate shipping and navigation on Inland Waterways declared by Parliament by Law to
 be national waterways. The responsibility and executive authority for development and maintenance of all waterways
 other than those declared as National Waterways rest with the State Governments. The following inland waterways

 have so far been declared as National Waterways through Acts of Parliament:
 
(i)                  Allahabad-Haldia stretch (1620 kms.) of the Ganga-Bhagirathi Hooghly river system by the National
 Waterways (Allahabad-Haldia stretch of Ganga-Hooghly river) Act, 1982
(ii)                Sadiya-Dhubri stretch (891 kms.) of Brahmputra river by the National Waterway (Sadiya-Dhubri stretch of
 the Brahmputra river) Act, 1988 ; and
(iii)               Kottapuram-Kollam stretch of the West Coast canal alongwith Champkara canal and Udyogmandal canal
 (205 kms.) by the National Waterway (Kollam-Kottapuram stretch of West Cost Canal and Champakara and
 Udyogmandal canal) Act, 1992.
3.1       The Central Government has constituted Inland Waterways Authority of India for development, maintenance
 and regulation of National Waterways for shipping and navigation. The infrastructure facilities on the existing three
 National Waterways are being created by it. It is aimed to made these three National Waterways fully functional by
 2007-08.
3.2       It is now proposed to declare Kakinada-Puducherry stretch of canals consisting of the Kakinada Canal, the Eluru
 Canal, the Commamur Canal, the Buckingham Canal and the Kaluvelly Tank, Bhadrachalam-Rajahmundry stretch of
 the Godavari river and Wazirabad-Vijayawada stretch of the Krishna river as National Waterway. (Annexure-I) The

3.3       The Department of Shipping informed that infrastructure currently available on this waterway is not adequate for
 safe, convenient and sustained shipping and navigation by large mechanized crafts. Therefore, the waterway is required
 to be developed by providing adequate infrastructure for safe, convenient and sustained shipping operations. It has been
 visualized that substantial quantum of inland water transport traffic to the tune of 6.42 million tones is likely to be
 carried on the proposed national waterway after its full development in a span of 5 years. This traffic is expected to be
 handled at 14 terminals namely Bhadrachalam, Pochavaram, Rajahmundry, Wazirabad, Muktiyala, Vijayawada, Eluru,
 Tadepalligudem, Kakinada, Kottapatnam, Maipadu, Durgajaupatnam, Chennai and Puducherry. The major identified
 cargo are paddy, tobacco, chilies, oil seeds, pulses and cotton; timber, bamboo, firewood, tendu (beedi) leaves, coal,
